title: Orbitaleve MarketKit GPU integration framing
next_steps: Redwood to share MarketKit + Private deployment one-pager and SOC2 summary (Maya) by 2025-11-30
Customer to provide rough perf targets (p50 latency, tokens/sec) and dataset size for pilot (Evan) by 2025-12-03
Schedule SE-led benchmark call with sample model (Jamal + Samir) week of 12/8
action_items: Maya: Send integration deck, private deployment checklist, and pricing ranges (due 2025-11-30)
Samir: Share current infra diagram and expected qps/peak windows (due 2025-12-03)
Jamal: Prepare short test plan for KV cache/batching trial (due 2025-12-05)
summary: Introductory partner discovery between Redwood and OrbitaLeve to assess MarketKit + GPU onramp integration. Focus on private/VPC options, routing/cost tradeoffs, and a small pilot scoped around a customer-facing search ranking use case. Customer has mixed on-prem + cloud infra and is sensitive to data residency and KMS integration.
topics: KV cache and batching behavior for ranking workload
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Good afternoon, everyone — thanks for making time. I'm Maya, AE on the channel team. Jamal from solutions is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Evan (OrbitaLeve): Good, thanks. Lina and Samir are here too. Appreciate you fitting this in.
[00:12] Lina: Hi all. Quick note, we have to keep this high level today but definitely want to land on next steps.
[00:18] Jamal (Redwood): Yep, totally. We'll go quick on the agenda: understand your MarketKit product, current infra, what success looks like, then map to Redwood's private and dedicated options.
[00:28] Evan: Sounds good. Briefly — OrbitaLeve builds the MarketKit orchestration layer for e-commerce search partners. We're trying to improve latency/cost for a ranking pipeline that does around 2k qps at peak across EU + US, also some regulatory requirements in EMEA. We're exploring GPU-accelerated inference to replace a CPU heavy ensemble.
[00:45] Samir: Right now it's a hybrid stack: most traffic on cloud instances but we have sensitive EU data that we want to keep in our VPC or on-prem racks.
[00:52] Maya: Okay that frames it well. Two quick clarifying questions: 1) are models proprietary or open? 2) is this a lift-and-shift or are you open to model quantization?
[01:03] Evan: Models are third-party open models plus a few in-house finetunes. We're open to quantization if quality holds — cost is a big driver.
[01:11] Lina: And we'll need KMS integration for key management, plus audit trails for compliance audits.
[01:15] Jamal: Totally expected. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and generates audit logs + SAML SSO. There may be some nuance re: key wrapping depending on your HSM.
[01:26] Evan: Can you run through how routing works if one of our regions loses capacity? We need graceful degradation.
[01:32] Maya: Sure. High level: we support policy-driven routing — you can prioritize region-local hosts, then fall back to other regions or a lower-cost quantized variant. Example: route to dedicated pools in region A, fallback to hosted in region B if capacity spikes.
[01:46] Samir: So fallback implies data transit. For EMEA we have strict rules. Is that configurable to avoid sending sensitive payloads outside the VPC?
[01:54] Jamal: Yes — you can set affinity policy to keep traffic local or to mask PII before fallback; there are options to block cross-border fallback entirely. That does impact availability though.
[02:06] Evan: Makes sense. What about perf — we need p50 around 60-80ms for short prompts in the ranking path. Is that realistic on a quantized LLM?
[02:16] Jamal: For short sequences and high batching, yes. The runtime supports continuous batching plus KV cache reuse. Quantized int8 / awq profiles can meet those latencies on modern Ampere/Blackwell GPUs depending on sequence length. There's some variance — we usually run a brief benchmark to pick kernel/quantization combination.
[02:36] Lina: Are there any models you recommend for ranking? We were looking at a trimmed GPT-style reranker and an open Bart variant.
[02:43] Jamal: Rerankers often do better as smaller encoder-decoder or cross-encoder models; they respond faster. For architecture parity, we usually recommend a narrow beam or a classifier-style rerank rather than full generative scoring to keep tokens and latency down.
[02:57] Evan: Understood. Let's talk integration patterns — do you have a deployable package for on-prem or is it API-first into our VPC?
[03:05] Maya: Two paths. For private customers you can either run a customer-managed control plane with Redwood agents in your VPC (we call that Private with VPC), or use our on-prem bundle where the control plane runs on your network. Both support pinned model versions, rollout policies, and mesh routing.
[03:21] Samir: Any infra prerequisites? We run a mixed fleet: a couple of A100 boxes on prem and G5/G6 in cloud.
[03:30] Jamal: We can support A100 and the newer Blackwell/RTX families. For best throughput you want consistent GPU types in a pool; mixing is supported but reduces predictability. Also note our kernels pick the best code path based on architecture; sometimes memory layout or NVLink changes perf.
[03:47] Evan: How intrusive is the agent? We have tight change control.
[03:51] Maya: The agent is lightweight — containerized, talk to local nvlink, exposes metrics to the control plane over TLS. You can run it behind your firewall and it only opens outbound to our control plane endpoints or your chosen control endpoint.
[04:04] Lina: Perfect. On security docs: do you have SOC2 and ISO artifacts?
[04:08] Maya: Yes. I'll send a SOC2 summary and the security pack. We also have a private deployment checklist that lists KMS, network ports, and audit log retention options.
[04:17] Samir: We'll need encryption at rest for model weights too — our procurement asks.
[04:22] Jamal: We support encrypted model storage with customer-managed keys in S3 or equivalent. On GPU nodes the in-memory keys are ephemeral and overwritten; we can detail the key lifecycle in the security pack.
[04:33] Evan: Quick question on billing. How do you think about usage for a hybrid pilot?
[04:38] Maya: For pilots we typically do short-term committed capacity or a blended pilot rate. Dedicated reserved pools are priced by GPU-hour plus delta for software; hosted per-token still exists as fallback. We'll include ranges in the deck.
[04:50] Lina: We have a procurement cadence — if pricing looks reasonable we can start a 3-month pilot. Timeline would be Jan for onboarding and Feb for pilot testing.
[04:59] Maya: Sounds good. Jamal, can you talk about the benchmark approach we recommend?
[05:03] Jamal: Sure. We prefer an SE-led bench: customer provides a representative payload set and a small evaluation harness. We run trials across a few quantization kernels, measure p50/p95, tokens/sec, and token-cost. We also exercise batching and KV cache with warm-up to reflect production. Typical run is 4–8 hours to get stable metrics.
[05:21] Evan: For our rerank flow, sampling needs to reflect short prompt and a cached prefix for the product context.
[05:26] Jamal: We'll do a warm-up phase to populate KV cache and then steady-state sampling. If you're doing cross-region routing we can simulate a region failure and measure fallbacks.
[05:36] Lina: Any red flags around model licensing? We use some apache2 and some permissive-licensed models.
[05:42] Jamal: Licensing is a customer-side check — Redwood doesn't relicense. We help operationalize whatever you choose, but we'll flag models we onboard that have usage caveats.
[05:51] Evan: Competitors — just to be transparent, we've chatted with Lambda Labs and CloudX. Two questions: 1) what differentiates Redwood vs Lambda? 2) How mature is your private on-prem runtime?
[06:03] Maya: Short answer: our differentiator is unified tooling and the routing/fallback primitives combined with an SE-friendly experience for production rollouts. Lambda is strong on raw self-hosting; Redwood emphasizes predictable economics (batching, caching knobs) plus observability. Runtime maturity — it's been in production for customers since 2023 across both cloud and some on-prem deployments.
[06:22] Samir: When you say observability what metrics are exposed?
[06:25] Jamal: Token-level latency, batch sizes, cache hit rates, per-model cost estimates, per-route error traces. We also export traces to your APM and offer per-tenant dashboards.
[06:36] Evan: We'd want to see example dashboards.
[06:38] Maya: I'll include screenshots and links to the console in the follow-up.
[06:43] Lina: Ok, two specific technical asks from our infra team: 1) what batching guarantees exist for low-latency paths? 2) how is the KV cache invalidated/consumed?
[06:54] Jamal: Batching is continuous with a configurable max latency threshold and max batch size. For low-latency routes you set max-latency to, say, 10ms to limit batching and prefer single shot with fallback to CPU if needed. KV cache is per-session, sharded across model instances; invalidation is TTL or explicit flush on model updates. There are also partial-prefix caching modes for rerankers.
[07:16] Samir: Partial-prefix caching — can you elaborate?
[07:18] Jamal: Instead of caching full context you can cache commonly repeated prefix token keys (e.g., product context) so the runtime reuses KV state for those tokens and only streams the variable portion. Helps cut compute for repeatable contexts.
[07:32] Evan: That seems promising for our product pages.
[07:35] Lina: For the pilot we'll likely want the private VPC model with a limited dedicated pool in EU. Can you outline the onboarding steps and typical lead times?
[07:44] Maya: Onboarding steps: security review -> network setup & KMS -> agent install on your nodes -> model pinning & baseline bench -> pilot run -> iterative tuning. Lead time is typically 2–6 weeks depending on procurement and access to nodes. For an EU-limited pilot we'd estimate 3–4 weeks if we get access quickly.
[08:02] Evan: Procurement is the gating factor. We'll aim to have PO & infra access by mid-December.
[08:08] Jamal: For the bench call, Samir, if you can provision a small A100 pool or give us a cloud project, we can run an initial smoke test.
[08:17] Samir: I can provision an A100 on our test rack; I'll confirm sizes in the action item.
[08:22] Maya: Great. Quick question — do you require model encryption at rest for weights in cloud? You mentioned procurement asks earlier.
[08:29] Lina: Yes, they'd prefer CMEK for storage.
[08:32] Jamal: Supported. We'll show the S3 SSE-KMS/CMEK flows in the security doc.
[08:39] Evan: Ok, one more pricing nuance: if we do dedicated pool plus hosted fallback what does blended billing look like?
[08:46] Maya: Blended pilots are two-part: reserved GPU hours at a discount, and fallback hosted calls billed at a per-token rate. We can model scenarios in a spreadsheet based on your qps and expected fallback rate. I'll include a sample cost model.
[08:59] Lina: That would be very helpful.
[09:01] Jamal: Also worth calling out the quantization tradeoffs: int4/int8 profiles save cost but sometimes increase variance in edge cases; we'll capture that in the bench results.
[09:12] Evan: Understood. Any limitations on model size for caching/sharding?
[09:16] Jamal: Larger models require more KV memory and sometimes multi-GPU sharding. We support sharded attention patterns but that increases complexity and warm-up time. For rerankers (smaller models) that complexity is less common.
[09:30] Samir: Do you have recommended batch sizes for A100 vs G6?
[09:35] Jamal: We'll provide a table after seeing sequence distribution, but ballpark: A100 can handle larger batch sizes and longer sequences; G6/G5 are great for smaller models and single-token latencies.
[09:47] Maya: I'm going to share a short checklist and an onboarding timeline in the follow-up.
[09:52] Evan: Quick ops question — how are model updates handled during pilot without downtime?
[09:57] Jamal: We support canary rollouts and automatic fallback to previous model versions. You can pin a percentage or use header-based routing for experiments.
[10:07] Lina: Great. Any considerations for audit/retention windows for logs?
[10:11] Maya: Configurable retention; default is 90 days, can be extended to 365+ on-prem. We'll include the options.
[10:19] Evan: For pilot scope let's nail three success metrics: p50 latency <= 80ms, sustained tokens/sec to handle 1.5k qps, and cost per 1M tokens less than current baseline by 30%.
[10:33] Maya: Helpful. We'll map metrics in the pilot plan.
[10:36] Samir: One more about telemetry — can we push to Datadog?
[10:39] Jamal: Yes, we ship metrics and traces to Datadog and other APMs.
[10:44] Lina: Ok, sounds like we have alignment.
[10:47] Maya: Quick recap and next steps: I'll send the security pack, onboarding checklist, and a cost model. Jamal will prepare the bench plan. Evan/Samir will share infra diagram and perf targets. We schedule the bench call for early December.
[11:01] Evan: Thanks, everyone. Looking forward to the docs.
[11:04] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up.
[11:06] [END - 11:06:30]

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-hearings around product names (MarketKit occasionally transcribed as Market Cat) and tech acronyms; timestamps approximate. Shared links referenced: Redwood private deployment one-pager (link to send), onboarding checklist (doc link), and a sample cost model spreadsheet (drive link).
notes: Customer is EU-sensitive; wants CMEK for storage and KMS integration. Pilot scoped to EU-limited dedicated pool with hosted fallback off by default for EMEA. Procurement timeline targets mid-December PO. SE-bench call next week of Dec 8 possible.
